nameStory: The 'shagbark' name becomes crystal clear the moment you see this tree's distinctive bark. As the hickory matures, its gray bark peels away in long, loose strips that curl outward at both ends, creating a wonderfully shaggy, unkempt appearance that looks like the tree is wearing a tattered coat.
description: Shagbark hickory is a large deciduous tree that can grow quite tall, with a straight trunk and rounded crown. Its most famous feature is the dramatically peeling bark that gives it its common name, though young trees have smooth bark that doesn't develop the 'shag' until they're older. The tree produces compound leaves with five leaflets and edible nuts that have been prized by both wildlife and humans for centuries.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: On mature trees, the gray bark peels away in long, loose strips that curl outward at both ends, creating a distinctly shaggy appearance. Young trees have smooth, tight bark that gradually develops the characteristic peeling as they age.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with exactly 5 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand. The three end leaflets are noticeably larger than the two bottom ones. Leaves feel slightly rough to the touch and turn golden-yellow in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round to oval nuts enclosed in a thick, four-sectioned husk that splits completely open when ripe. The husk is green when young, turning brown and woody. The sweet, edible nut inside has a hard shell.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Large, egg-shaped buds that are quite noticeable in winter. The buds have overlapping scales and can be up to an inch long, much larger than most other tree buds you'll encounter.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a large, stately tree with a straight trunk and rounded crown. Branches tend to be strong and don't droop, giving the tree an upright, dignified appearance even when leafless.

habitat: Shagbark hickory thrives in rich, well-drained soils of mixed hardwood forests throughout New England, though it's more common in the southern parts of the region. You'll often find it growing alongside oaks, maples, and other hickories on slopes and well-drained bottomlands. It prefers full sun to partial shade and can tolerate various soil types as long as drainage is good.

seasonality.spring: Small, inconspicuous yellowish-green flowers appear in drooping clusters as leaves emerge. The large buds are very noticeable before leaves unfurl, and new leaves emerge with a fresh, bright green color.
seasonality.summer: Full canopy provides dense shade with the characteristic 5-leaflet compound leaves. Young green nuts begin developing and bark shows its full shaggy character on mature trees.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn beautiful golden-yellow before dropping. Nuts ripen and fall, with their thick husks splitting open to reveal the edible nuts inside - a busy time for squirrels and other wildlife.
seasonality.winter: The distinctive shaggy bark is most visible and impressive against snow. Large, prominent buds and strong branching pattern make identification possible even without leaves.

funFact: Native Americans discovered that shagbark hickory nuts are so rich in oil that they could boil them in water to create 'hickory milk' - a nutritious, creamy liquid that was stored in gourds and used like dairy milk throughout winter.
confusionNotes: Young shagbark hickories with smooth bark can be tricky to distinguish from other hickories, but remember the '5-leaflet rule' - shagbark always has exactly 5 leaflets while pignut hickory typically has 5-7 and mockernut has 7-9. Once the bark starts peeling in those distinctive long strips, identification becomes unmistakable.
contextualKnowledge: The wood of shagbark hickory is incredibly strong and flexible, making it the preferred wood for tool handles, baseball bats, and drumsticks. Early American settlers quickly learned from Native Americans that hickory wood burns hot and slow, making it ideal for smoking meats - giving us the famous 'hickory-smoked' flavor we know today.
compareHints: Among New England's hickories, shagbark is the only one with bark that peels in long, dramatic strips - other hickories have tight, furrowed bark. Its exactly-5-leaflets also help distinguish it from mockernut hickory (7-9 leaflets) and sometimes pignut hickory (5-7 leaflets). Bitternut hickory also has fewer leaflets but has distinctive yellow buds and different bark patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England hickories, bitternut is the easiest to identify thanks to its unique yellow buds.
Pignut hickory has much smoother bark than the dramatically peeling shagbark hickory, and smaller, less noticeable buds than the large, fuzzy-budded mockernut hickory.

Among New England hickories, mockernut is the only one with consistently fuzzy leaf undersides - shagbark hickory has peeling bark plates, bitternut has bright yellow buds, and pignut has smooth leaves and smaller nuts.

Red hickory differs from shagbark hickory by having smooth bark instead of distinctive shaggy plates, and from pignut hickory by typically having 5 leaflets instead of 7, plus sweeter nuts and reddish inner bark.
Among New England hickories, shellbark stands out for its larger nuts and more dramatic bark peeling compared to shagbark hickory.
